content.thinking:
This environment seems to be a read-only replay where some commands refuse to run, so I should test whether writes actually work before committing to a design. Let me try creating a file first to confirm, then sketch out the pixel-based model.

For the subject: a koala clinging to a eucalyptus branch mounted on a stand base. I'm working out the pose - maybe a vertical trunk with a stump base and side branch with leaves, koala hugging the trunk with arms and gripping with hind legs. I need to think through orientation carefully since the koala's face should be visible to the viewer, not hidden behind the trunk, so I'm considering having it sit in a fork or on an angled branch with front paws gripping forward instead.

I'm leaning toward simplifying: skip the awkward fork-sitting pose and instead keep limbs separated and extended in a clean, readable rest pose, with the koala sitting upright and just lightly contacting the branch rather than fully wrapping around it for legibility.

I'm settling on a clearer pose instead: the koala sits upright on a horizontal branch with hind legs wrapped around it, while its arms stretch forward and up to grip a thinner overhead branch at face level, keeping the head and limbs clearly readable.

Now I'm working out the stand structure—an octagonal stump base with pixel bark texture supporting a leaning main trunk, with a thick side branch extending forward for the koala to sit on, and figuring out exact coordinates and sizing for the koala relative to this setup.

I'll make the base a stepped pixel-art octagon stump with bark texture and mossy top. For the trunk, I'm placing it leaning slightly behind the koala at x=-0.15, z=-0.2, tapering upward, with a horizontal seat branch extending forward so the koala can sit with its back resting against the trunk.

Now I'm positioning the koala's limbs: thighs splayed forward-out to grip the branch, feet gripping near the branch's front end around x=±0.06, with knees positioned slightly wider to give a natural seated straddle.

For the arms, I'm adding a second curved branch above reaching forward from the trunk toward the koala's chest height, and figuring out the torso proportions (rump, shoulders, head) so the arms can plausibly stretch up and grip that upper branch.

Right, the ears stick out to x=0.2 so I need to widen the arm path to avoid collision—spreading hands to x=±0.17 on the branch with shoulders at ±0.15, routing elbows outward before curving up to the hands, keeping ears positioned at x=±0.12 near the top of the head.

I'm weighing an overhead branch versus one at chest height; overhead wins because it frames the face with leaves, so I'll thicken that upper branch and scatter leaf cards on its tip and the trunk top. I'm also planning the koala's fur details—fluffy white ear fringes, a white chest patch, grey body fur with brown pelt texture.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton structure: hips as root, a spine chain, neck and head with a separate small jaw box, arm chains with shoulder-elbow-wrist-hand (including koala-style opposable thumb digits), legs, hinged ears, and just a tiny tail stub since koalas lack tails. I'm also deciding whether to render the body with blocky sweep sections to keep that chunky pixel-art look rather than smooth tubes.

I'm working out texel density and paint sheet sizing so the cellPaint texture reads crisply at koala scale, leaning toward a 1024px sheet with roughly 1.6cm texels, and considering low-segment ellipsoids for the rounded head shape while keeping the pixel art cells square-ish per face.

For facial features I'm planning tiny decals for the eyes with nearest-filtering pixel textures, and for the nose I'm thinking of using a squashed box part with a simple pixel-art texture showing a dark spoon shape plus a highlight pixel, applying the same drawing to all faces rather than fussing over tiled cropping.

For fur I'm scattering small pixel-tuft cards across the torso and limbs for a fuzzy silhouette, adding white rim tufts along the ears, cheeks, and chest, and using tinted color variants of the tuft texture to keep the atlas small. Now I'm starting to think through bark detailing for the eucalyptus branch, like vertical peeling strip patterns painted onto the surface.

For the branch I'm mottling the bark with cream, grey, and tan patches to mimic smooth gum tree bark, then adding sickle-shaped blue-green leaf cards plus rounder juvenile leaves and small gumnut pods hung off branch stubs with lean rotations. For the base I'm making a stump slice with concentric growth rings on top, bark texture on the sides, scattered moss patches, a few fallen leaf cards, and maybe a tiny engraved nameplate.

I'm considering stamping "KOALA" in a tiny 3x5 pixel font on a small plaque tilted on the front edge of the base. Sizing-wise I'm settling on an octagonal stump base around 0.5m radius with the trunk rising to about 1.35m total, giving a compact koala-in-a-eucalyptus display with a broken top and leafy side branches.

For the skeleton, I need exactly one root joint, so I'm making hips the root since static tree/stand parts would otherwise attach to whichever koala bone is nearest and tear apart during posing. Assigning the stand parts to the hips bone keeps the whole tree rigid and moving together when the hips are posed.

Now I'm laying out the spine chain from hips upward through mid-back to chest, curving slightly forward to match a koala sitting upright against the tree.

Then I'm positioning the neck and head joint, sizing the skull larger and wider to match a koala's proportions, with the muzzle pushed forward for the nose area.

Now I'm placing the flat koala face with the spoon-shaped nose protruding on top, sizing the muzzle box and nose separately, then adding the lower jaw as a small forward-facing box joined at the chin. For the torso, I'm planning a pear-shaped loft along the spine chain with wider hip radii tapering toward the shoulders.

Writing sweep code...

Actually that's fine — the koala sitting on the branch should overlap naturally, sinking into the fur, so I'll adjust hips to y=0.40 with a rump radius of 0.13, giving a bottom around 0.27, letting the branch (centered at y=0.25) tuck slightly into the fur for a believable seated pose.

Now I'm working out how the legs wrap around the branch: feet resting on top with toes curling over the front edge, positioning ankles and toe joints so they clear the branch's top surface, and extending the branch itself further along z with a chunky cut end cap for a natural look. I'm also checking the thigh and shin proportions by computing the hip-to-knee and knee-to-ankle distances to make sure the leg geometry stays proportional.

For the actual skeleton, I'm planning to use a three-point chain (hip, knee, ankle) with matching joint names so the ankle becomes the tip joint, then attach a separate foot structure with toe chains as digits -- aiming for four toes plus an opposable big toe per hind foot, mirrored for the hands, bringing the total joint count to around sixty. Now I'm placing the shoulder and starting the elbow position for the arms.

For the arms holding the branch, I'm reconsidering the branch geometry entirely -- rather than running toward the viewer along z, the upper branch should curve out from the trunk and run horizontally across in front of the face like a monkey bar, spanning roughly x=-0.45 to 0.45 at a fixed height and depth, so the hands can grip it symmetrically at mirrored x positions.

Maybe simpler: a V-shaped fork from the trunk, each branch curving forward and outward, with each koala hand gripping one side of the fork.

Checking that ears sit near x±0.13 and the branch tip clears that zone, I work out arm placement: shoulder to hand spans roughly 0.35 with the elbow bent outward for a natural pose.

Verifying segment lengths against the shoulder-hand distance, and checking elbow clearance past the ear disc — the z-gap is wide enough to avoid collision. Now adding a cream-colored belly patch to the torso before moving to the head.

I'm picturing a cute touch: a eucalyptus leaf tucked in the koala's mouth corner. For the branch, I'm placing leaf clusters along the forked tips and extra twigs, with each leaf card oriented to hang straight down from its attachment point.

For the trunk, I want upper portions with side twigs and foliage, plus lower details like knots, peeling bark, a hollow knothole, moss, and maybe tiny ants. At the base I'm adding ground clutter: fallen leaves, a mushroom cluster, small fern tufts, pebbles, fallen gumnuts, and a plaque on the stand. For the koala's fur, I'm planning a grey base tone with a darker back, lighter ears, a white chest tuft, and brownish dithering for texture.

I'm limiting the palette to flat colors under 64, with a five-step grey ramp for fur shading plus dithering based on surface normal, noise, and zone (lighter belly). I'm giving the chest a cream-white patch and darkening the hands and claws, then scattering fur tuft cards across the torso, arms, thighs, head, and ear rims to build out the surface texture.

Designing tuft texture pixels...

Now thinking about the ear shape: a flattened sphere scaled and rotated outward, with a lighter inner face suggesting cream/white fur and a grey outer rim with white tufts along the edge.

For the eyes, I'm sketching a tiny pixel-art pattern for round black koala eyes with a small highlight, placed symmetrically on the skull at an angle, then moving to the nose as a dark rounded box built from stepped pixel shapes.

Still designing the nose texture, but realizing alpha-cut pixel patterns on a solid box geometry would expose the hollow interior through the transparent corners, so I'm reconsidering and leaning toward opaque pixel colors with a plain box shape instead.

Instead I'll use a low-poly sphere with a shaded gradient highlight for the nose rather than a box with cutouts, applying a dark ramp by surface normal with dithering for a cel-shaded look. I'm settling on consistent pixel scale constants and estimating the overall part budget, then starting to plan the hand geometry with opposable thumbs and gripping fingers built from small palm boxes.

Each digit uses a two-joint chain from a three-point path, giving five digits per side times two joints times two sides for roughly 40 finger joints across front and hind limbs, plus about 25 for the body, keeping the total well under budget. I'm working out how the hand wraps around the branch, with the palm resting on top and fingers curling down the front while thumbs grip from behind, oriented along the branch's direction at that point.

Still working out the finger-wrap geometry...

Working out the orthonormal frame for each hand's grip, computing tangent and outward vectors so the fingers wrap correctly on each side of the branch...

Planning the finger geometry: a three-point curve running below the branch, out to the side, then over the top, giving a natural curled grip shape, with thin claw spikes added at the tips and a capsule shape for the palm resting against the branch.

For the arm, I'm chaining shoulder-elbow-wrist down to the branch, then thinking through hind foot placement -- since the branch runs along z, the hind feet need to sit slightly offset in x on either side, wrapping toes over the top to look like a proper grip.

Still working out toe placement...

Continuing to knee and ankle positions, checking that the leg lengths stay plausible and the ankle sits right at the branch top for the frog-like splayed pose, then verifying the torso's hip radius clears the branch surface.

Now I'm working out the trunk's curve so it sways slightly and tapers from base to top, then checking clearance between the koala's torso and the trunk — I find they overlap, so I adjust the trunk's position and radius back to fix the collision.

Next I'm plotting the seat branch and the forked branches as rod-like curves extending from the trunk toward the hands, solving for coordinates so the shoulders and hand positions align along that forked path.

I notice the ear position collides with the branch at that height, so I'm raising the fork's base and lengthening the arms to clear the overlap.

That's close enough with slight bending, so I'll nudge the ear position lower and rearward for clearance from the branch. The head size checks out against real koala proportions, and overall height with the leaves looks fine, so I'm ready to move on to actually writing the code.

I'm setting up the imports from the builder, math, path, and pixel-paint utilities, then checking the type signatures for cellPaint, pick, and the Builder object before using them. Now I'm defining the fur paint function, sampling noise and normal direction to shade the texel colors.

I'm figuring out how to detect the belly region in model space using normal direction and position thresholds, with added noise for a ragged fur edge, and mapping out the koala's realistic coloring scheme—grey-brown back, white chest/belly, white inner ears, and spotted white-brown rump patches.

For the stump, I'm planning the eucalyptus bark texture using cell-based painting with vertically stretched noise to create elongated bark patches in cream, grey-green, tan-pink, and orange tones, plus concentric ring patterns for the stump's top face based on radial distance from center.

Now I'm figuring out the stepped-octagon extrusion to approximate a circular stump cross-section: computing per-column half-heights using the circle equation to get a pixelated disc outline, then extruding that profile along the vertical axis.

I'll build a layered base instead: a mossy soil skirt, then a log-slice stump with bark sides and a ring-patterned top, sized to sit the koala/branch centered at the origin.

Writing blob span generator...

For bark texture I'm thinking rods with 8 sides for the trunk and 6 for twigs, adding dark knot patches, small tilted peeling-bark strips in cream and orange along the trunk, and dark vertical scar lines.

Now I'm figuring out the leaf cards: a sickle-shaped eucalyptus leaf texture drawn narrow and curved with a lighter mid-rib, oriented so the root attaches at the top and the tip hangs down, accounting for how the card's 180-degree lean flips the drawing when viewed from downstream.

For gumnuts, I'll build tiny brown capsule shapes using small spheres with a darker lid disc, merging geometries by bone and color to keep part count manageable—aiming to stay under roughly 700 total parts. Now I'm planning where to place leaf clusters, positioning frames at each branch tip and twig.

For the leaf cards, I'm working out the flow direction and lean angle so each leaf hangs naturally from its twig, with the face orientation determining whether the drawn side reads correctly from the viewer's position—since cards are double-sided, I'll just accept mirrored leaves where they occur. To add variety I'll randomize the flow direction horizontally and spin each leaf around its axis so facings differ across the cluster, while keeping lean within a consistent range across the whole plant.

For twig leaf placement, I'm sweeping a thin catmull curve from each branch point outward and downward, then framing 4-7 leaves along it with lean 180 so they hang straight down, varying leaf size in 2-3 scales for a natural clustered look. I also want to add a leaf sticking out of the koala's mouth, framed at the mouth point with a forward-upward direction and lean 0 so it points straight out rather than hanging.

Now I'm turning to the ears -- big round fuzzy shapes attached at hinge joints on the head bone, built from scaled ellipsoid spheres oriented so their thin axis points outward and slightly forward, positioning the left ear mirrored for the right.

For the ear interiors I'm layering in a smaller cream sphere offset slightly forward, then adding a ring of white tuft cards around the ear rim for that fuzzy fringe, with the cards leaning outward along the radial direction. I'm also planning cheek tufts as scattered white fluffy cards on the sides of the face, filtered to positions away from center and below the top of the head.

Now I'm figuring out body fur tufts via torso scatter filtered by normal direction, tinting cards using the fur paint evaluated at each card root for color consistency, layering grey textures with multiply tint for shading. Next I'll move on to building the arm chain and hand geometry with vector math helper functions.

Setting up the skeleton builder, defining the root joint, and establishing a spine chain using a catmull-rom curve through hip, spine, and chest positions with named joints along the path.

I'm then extending the rig upward with neck and head joints, building a short path from the chest's top position toward the head base and naming the segments accordingly.

Now I'm working out the torso sweep geometry, defining a radius function that varies along the spine chain to shape the tube's cross-section with the normal direction oriented properly for a vertical, slightly bending torso.

Shifting spine points up slightly: hips at 0.40, chest region to 0.65, chest end 0.71, with neck joint at 0.71 and head joint/center around 0.77-0.82. Now working out torso side count and head shaping details.

Building the skull as a scaled sphere positioned on the head bone, then shaping the muzzle as a broad flat-ish shape separate from the jaw, and placing a large protruding nose typical of a koala's snout at the top-front of the muzzle with black cell shading.

For the jaw, I'm attaching it to its own joint below the muzzle so it can animate open/close, using a cream-colored scaled sphere, and considering a thin dark slab to visually close the mouth gap between upper and lower parts since the pieces don't perfectly meet. Next I need to work out the eyes as decals on the skull.

Now I'm placing dark eyes with highlights at symmetric angles on the skull surface, skipping the subtle eye-ring detail koalas have, then adding fur tufts around the cheeks, top of head, forehead, and chin.

For the arms, I need to find where the hand grips the branch by computing the closest point along the branch's curve path and extracting its tangent direction, then set up the two forks (left and right, mirrored) as tapered sweeps from a thicker base to a narrower tip.

I'm defining a hand coordinate frame at each branch point with up and outward vectors, then laying out three fingers and two thumbs along the branch tangent on opposite sides to create a realistic gripping pose, with the palm and wrist positioned below and behind the branch toward the arm.

Working out the three-point curve for each finger wrapping under, around, and over the branch, with tapering radius toward the clawed tip curling inward.

For the thumb, I'm mirroring the finger path toward the inner side, checking that its position relative to the head and ear doesn't cause overlap.

Now I need to name the finger joint chains properly so they match the expected naming pattern for each side.

Still defining limb chains...

I'm checking whether the foot rests properly on top of the branch given its center and radius, and working out that the toes need to wrap around the sides of the branch rather than spreading along its length, so the foot orientation should point across the branch axis.

Writing hind foot toe geometry...

Still shaping toe curves...

For the foot pad, I'm connecting ankle to toe bases with a capsule sweep and adding wide pad boxes for each toe, then planning a similar palm structure for the hand using a capsule from the wrist.

Now I'm adding small claw spikes at each digit tip, oriented along the tangent direction of the digit chain, plus static twig details, belly and chest coloring, and rump spotting for body texture.

Then I'm listing out the texture cards needed: grey and cream fur tufts (tinted variants of one base texture), colored leaf and round-leaf cards, bark peel, grass tufts, reused leaf cards for fallen leaves, and fluffy eucalyptus blossom pom-poms as a small starburst card.

I'm designing a tiny pixel font (3x5 grid per letter) to spell "KOALA" for a plaque, laying out the letter patterns and sizing the overall plaque texture with margins, then planning to render it as a decal plane in front of a brass/wood plate rather than wrapping a full box texture.

For the physical plaque, I'm considering mounting options against the stump's rounded front edge, settling on a tilted plate propped on a small sloped wooden wedge block near the base of the stump.

Rotating the box 35° about X achieves that same tilt, so I'll just set rotation [35,0,0] directly instead of computing a dir vector. Now I'm working out the stump's footprint radius versus the koala's scale to make sure proportions look right.

Reducing the stump radius to roughly 0.44m with center offset, placing the plaque and seat branch so nothing overlaps near the rim. Checking the overall bounding extents of base, trunk, and branch tips to confirm the model stays compact, then planning root buttress flares and moss details at the base.

Before writing the actual build code, I want to verify the type signatures in kits/pixel.ts for cellPaint, pick, Cell, and the pixelArt function, plus check how parts, sticks, cards, and decals are structured in src/builder, along with frame imports and surface scatter hits -- so I'll grep the relevant exports first.

input.command: cd ~/tmp-archive/sonnet-100/koalaSonnet && grep -n "export" kits/pixel.ts && sed -n 1,80p src/frame.ts && grep -n "cards\|decal\|stick(" src/builder.ts | head -20
